gallery.credit: Walters Art Museum:  Home page  Info about artwork
gallery.source: Interior of a Mosque at Cordova
gallery.description: This work, set in the 8th-century Great Mosque of Cordova in Spain may have been begun in 1880 while Weeks was staying in that city. In Weeks' estate sale catalogue, the scene was described as follows: Preaching the holy war against the Christians, the old Moor holds aloft the green flag of Mohammed while he curses the "dogs of Christians" with true religious fervor, and calls upon the followers of Mohammed to drive them out of Spain.
categories: American paintings in the Walters Art Museum

gallery.filename: Cathedral–Mosque of Córdoba (6933169868).jpg
gallery.title: File:Cathedral–Mosque of Córdoba (6933169868).jpg
gallery.source: Cathedral–Mosque of Córdoba (6933169868)
gallery.description:
The Cathedral and former Great Mosque of Córdoba, in ecclesiastical terms the Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción (English: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption), and known by the inhabitants of Córdoba as the Mezquita-Catedral (Mosque–Cathedral), is today a World Heritage Site and the cathedral of the Diocese of Córdoba. It is located in the Andalusian city of Córdoba, Spain. The site was originally a pagan temple, then a Visigothic Christian church, before the Umayyad Moors at first converted the building into a mosque and then built a new mosque on the site. After the Spanish Reconquista, it once again became a Roman Catholic church, with a plateresque cathedral later inserted into the centre of the large Moorish building. The Mezquita is regarded as the one of the most accomplished monuments of Islamic architecture.

Cathedral–Mosque of Córdoba. (2012, April 2). In Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. Retrieved 09:09, April 15, 2012, from en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cathedral%E2%80%93Mosq...

gallery.title: File:Córdoba 2015 10 23 2733 (25613751954).jpg
gallery.artist: Harvey Barrison from Massapequa, NY, USA
gallery.description: In 1236, Córdoba was conquered by King Ferdinand III of Castile, and the mosque was converted into a Catholic church and over time taking the name Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba. Alfonso X oversaw the construction of the Villaviciosa Chapel and the Royal Chapel within the mosque. The kings who followed added further Christian features, such as King Henry II rebuilding the chapel in the 14th century.

gallery.description: Se comenzó a construir en el año 786 sobre una basílica visigoda anterior. Se amplió y reformó en sucesivas ocasiones durante el Emirato y el Califato de Córdoba. Midió más de 23000 metros cuadrados, lo que la convirtió en la segunda mezquita del mundo, tras la Mezquita de La Meca. En el siglo XIII se produjo la reconquista cristiana de Córdoba y se convirtió en la catedral de la diócesis.

gallery.filename: Plano de la Mezquita de Córdoba (revised with labels and dates).jpg
gallery.title: File:Plano de la Mezquita de Córdoba (revised with labels and dates).jpg
gallery.credit: Wiki Commons: Plano de la Mezquita de Córdoba.jpg
gallery.source: Plano de la Mezquita de Córdoba (revised with labels and dates)
gallery.description:
This is a slightly revised version of a previously uploaded floor plan image (Plano de la Mezquita de Córdoba.jpg). The main revisions are: 1) extended the color scheme distinctions to the courtyard section, 2) removed a couple of faint labels and two other features in courtyard which don't show up in representations of the historical mosque's floor plan, 3) rotated image so the north and south ends are at the top and bottom respectively, 4) added names of Muslim rulers who built each section and the starting date of construction (which sometimes varies according to sources, hence the wide range specified for Abd ar-Rahman II).


The information here (revisions, dates, and all) is in line with the information and equivalent illustrations provided in Jonathan Bloom's recent book "Architecture of the Islamic West: North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula, 700-1800" (2020), which is a reliable summary of existing scholarly research. Note: The only detail which I believe may be missing, based on a reading of sources, is that there should be a gallery of arches and columns running around the edge of the courtyard as of Abd ar-Rahman III's extension.
